unit.title: Money and inflation
unit.description: What money is, why it loses value and how it grows with compound interest

texts: Two salaries, two endings
Marta
Pablo
Marta earns €1,800 a month. Pablo, €1,300.
This month I bought some new trainers, ate out three times… and I've still got €50 left over!
I cook at home nearly all the time. I've got €300 left over and I put it aside.
In 5 years' time, without investing anything, who'll have more saved?
Marta, because she earns more
Marta puts aside €50 a month: **€3,000** in 5 years. Pablo puts aside €300: **€18,000**, six times as much.
Pablo, because he puts more aside each month
Exactly! Pablo builds up **€18,000** in 5 years and Marta €3,000. What counts is what you keep, not what you earn.
Both the same
No: Marta puts aside €50 a month and Pablo €300. In 5 years that's €3,000 versus €18,000.
Earning a lot isn't the same as **having** a lot. Let's measure what Pablo has.
How much does he really have?
This is what Pablo owns and what he owes. Place each item: does it **add** or **subtract**?
Pablo's net worth
What he owns
What he owes
Savings in the bank
The money he's saved is his: it adds.
His car (what it's worth today)
What you own counts at what it's worth today, not what it cost.
What's left on the car loan
A debt subtracts: the car isn't fully his yet.
His laptop
Something valuable adds, even if it's worth a bit less every year.
His unpaid card balance
What you owe on your card subtracts, even if you can't see it.
Place everything and find out Pablo's net worth.
**Net worth = what you own − what you owe.** Pablo's: 9,500 − 4,300 = **€5,200**. It's a snapshot; his income and savings are the film that keeps changing it.
Watch out for debts: even if you can't see them, they subtract.
You're doing well! Watch how the sum below changes.
Tap **add** or **subtract** for each item

steps.title: What money is for
steps.body:
Money does three jobs:

• **Means of payment:** you swap work for bread without bartering.
• **Unit of account:** you know a coffee is worth less than a bike.
• **Store of value:** you can keep it for tomorrow… although, as you'll see in the next lesson, it slowly wears away.
steps.key: Wealth is net worth, not salary: what you own minus what you owe.

texts: Grandma's 100 pesetas
Grandma Carmen
When I was your age, I'd come back from the market with a full basket for 100 pesetas.
Today 100 pesetas would be 60 cents. That wouldn't even get you a loaf of bread!
Why do you think that is?
Because things used to be lower quality
Quality has changed a bit, but that doesn't explain why **everything** goes up: bread is still bread.
Because prices go up a little every year and it builds up
That's it! It's called **inflation**. 3 % a year sounds like nothing… until 20 years go by.
Because the euro is worth less than the peseta
The exchange rate was 166.386 pesetas to the euro: that's not the problem. What matters is how much prices have risen since then.
Well, let's see if you understand it better than I do
Let's look at it with your own shopping basket.
Your basket in a few years
Today, **€50** gets you this whole basket. But prices go up every year with inflation…
Bread
Milk
Fruit
Pasta
Eggs
Chicken
Fish
Olive oil
Coffee
With 3 % inflation a year, what will those same €50 get you in 20 years' time?
Almost everything: 3 % is very little
About half the basket
Nothing: everything will cost ten times as much
3 % for 20 years pushes prices up by 81 %: your €50 buys what €28 buys today. Check it by moving the years.
Find the inflation rate that halves your basket in just 10 years.
A trick to work it out in your head: **70 ÷ inflation** = years until your money buys half as much. At 7 %, 10 years; at 2 %, 35.
Oof! That doesn't even fill a third of the basket. That's what high inflation feels like.
See? The notes are the same €50, but they buy much less.
Now turn the inflation up: what happens at 7 %?
Drag the years and see what happens to your basket

steps.title: Why prices go up
steps.body:
They rise when there's more money or more demand than things to buy, or when producing costs more (energy in 2022). In Spain it's measured by the INE (the national statistics office) with the **CPI**: in 2025 it averaged 2.7 %.

The ECB tries to keep it around **2 %** by raising or cutting interest rates.
steps.key: With inflation, money that sits still buys a little less every year.

u1l3.title: The CPI and your shopping basket

texts: Why do I notice it more?
Leo
Sara
They say inflation is 3 %, but I feel like everything's going up way more than that.
Well, I barely notice it…
Leo rents a flat and drives everywhere. Sara lives with her family and gets around by bike.
This year, rent and petrol have gone up more than everything else. Who's right?
Leo's exaggerating: inflation is the same for everyone
The CPI is an **average**. Everyone has their own basket: if you spend more on what's rising most, your inflation is higher.
Both: each of them has their own inflation
That's it! The CPI is everyone's average. Leo spends a lot on rent and petrol, so **his** inflation is higher than 3 %.
Sara: if she doesn't notice it, there's no inflation
Just because Sara doesn't notice it doesn't mean prices aren't rising: her basket has less of what has gone up most.
The inflation that doesn't move as much
The INE gives two figures. **Headline CPI** measures the whole basket. **Core inflation** strips out what goes up and down very fast (energy and fresh food) to show the underlying trend.
Counts in core
Left out: very volatile
The electricity bill
It's energy: it can shoot up one month and drop the next.
A T-shirt
Clothes change price bit by bit: they count in core.
Fresh strawberries
Unprocessed food depends on the weather and the harvest: it's left out.
A haircut
Services change slowly: they're the underlying trend.
Filling up the tank
Fuel is energy: very volatile.
A packet of pasta
It's processed food: it stays in core.
Sort all six items.
If electricity shoots up one month, headline CPI jumps, but **core** barely moves. That's why central banks watch it so closely: it shows the underlying trend.
Hint: anything that depends on the weather or on oil is out.
In or out? Sort each item

steps.title: How it's measured
steps.body:
Every month, the INE records the prices of a **basket** of hundreds of goods and services: food, housing, transport, leisure… The **CPI** is how much that basket has changed compared with the same month a year earlier.

Each item is weighted by what households spend on it on average.
steps.key: The CPI is everyone's average: your inflation depends on what you spend on.

texts: Safe… or protected?
You have **€10,000** in an account that pays 0 %. The balance never goes down. But prices go up…
With 2.7 % inflation a year, what will those €10,000 buy in 10 years' time?
The same: the balance hasn't gone down
What about €7,700 buys today
What about €2,700 buys today
Over 10 years at 2.7 %, prices rise by 31 %: your €10,000 buys what €7,661 buys today. You don't lose euros, you lose **purchasing power**.
How much would the account need to pay so you don't lose purchasing power?
**Real return ≈ return − inflation.** You only gain purchasing power if your money earns more than prices go up.
Yikes! Your money shrinks really fast like this.
Still in the red: your euros are growing more slowly than prices.
Raise what the account pays until the line stops falling
«They're safe there»
Uncle Javi
I've had €20,000 in my account for years. At 0 %, but I'm not losing anything there.
What do you say to him?
You're right, the balance doesn't go down
The balance doesn't go down, but with 2.5 % inflation, in 15 years that €20,000 will buy what about **€13,800** buys today.
Safe, yes, but every year they buy a bit less
Well spotted! He's not losing euros: he's losing **purchasing power**. Whatever he won't need for years can be put to work to beat inflation.
Better take it out and keep it at home
In a drawer it loses out to inflation just the same… and it can get lost or stolen too.
Huh… I'd never thought of it like that.

Bear in mind: deposits are protected up to **€100,000** by the Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos (Spain's deposit guarantee scheme) if the bank goes bust. That protects your euros, not your purchasing power.
The mattress, simple and compound

Three ways to keep **€1,000**:

• **Under the mattress:** it doesn't grow.
• **Simple interest:** you always earn on what you put in.
• **Compound interest:** you also earn on what you've already earned.
€1,000 at 7 % a year for 30 years. How much will you have with compound interest?
About €3,100
About €7,600
About €21,000
With simple interest it would be €3,100. With compound, **€7,612**: almost two and a half times as much, without adding a single euro.
Reach €10,000 without adding any money: play with the return and the years.
Compounding **speeds up**: the last years grow much more than the first ones. That's why time matters as much as the return.
Returns that high aren't normal: 7 % is already very good over the long term.
Look at the end of the green curve: it shoots up!
Move the years: watch how the lines pull apart
Ana and Bruno
Both put aside **€200 a month** at 7 % until 65. Ana starts at 25. What if Bruno starts later?
Ana
Bruno
Bruno starts 10 years after Ana. At 65, how much will he have compared with her?
25 % less
Less than half
Almost the same
Ana ends up with about **€494,000** and Bruno with about **€234,000**: less than half, even though Ana only put in €24,000 more.
Delay Bruno until Ana has three times as much as him.
Every year you wait costs far more than it seems: your first euros are the ones with the most time to compound.
Starting at 45, Bruno can't catch up with Ana even if he puts in the same each month.
If they start at the same time, they end up the same. Now delay Bruno
Every year of delay widens the gap. How far does it go?

steps.title: It works against you too
steps.body:
Compound interest works the same way with debt: a card that charges interest on interest grows on its own. You'll see it in the debt unit.

And remember: these are examples, not promises. The stock market doesn't return 7 % every year.
steps.key: Gains generate new gains: the sooner you start, the more time works for you.

texts: When does it double?
There's a trick to work out in your head how long your money takes to double: **72 ÷ return**.
At 6 % a year, how many years does it take for €1,000 to double?
In 6 years
In about 12 years
In about 20 years
72 ÷ 6 = **12 years**. The exact maths gives 11.9: the rule of 72 is almost spot on.
Find the return that doubles your money in about 8 years.
**72 ÷ return = years to double.** And the other way round: 72 ÷ years = the return you need.
This works for debt too: a card at 24 % doubles what you owe in 3 years.
At 2 %, 36 years to double! That's about what inflation usually runs at…
Move the return and watch the stack of notes grow
An incredible offer
Nico
I've found a fund that **doubles your money in 2 years** with no risk. Are you in? Places are only open today.
Use the rule of 72. What do you think?
I'm in! Sounds amazing
Doubling in 2 years means **36 % a year** (72 ÷ 2). Nobody can guarantee that «with no risk»: it has all the hallmarks of a scam.
72 ÷ 2 = 36 % a year with no risk: impossible. Smells like a scam
Spot on! A guaranteed 36 % a year doesn't exist. And the rush («today only») is another classic sign of a scam.
I'll ask him to explain it and go in with half
Better not to risk even half: 36 % a year «with no risk» is impossible. Check the CNMV (Spain's market regulator) website first.
The rule of 72 is your nonsense detector: if the promised return is huge and «safe», be suspicious.

u1l1-1.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
u1l1-1.explanation: Income and savings are flows (every month); net worth is a snapshot at one moment.
right: What you don't spend of what comes in
What you own minus what you owe
Putting savings to work to produce more

u1l1-2.prompt: You have €2,500 in the bank and a laptop worth €800, and you owe €1,200 on a loan. What's your net worth?
u1l1-2.explanation: 2,500 + 800 − 1,200 = €2,100. Net worth subtracts what you owe.

u1l1-3.prompt: Which of these functions of money breaks down when inflation is high?
options: Unit of account to compare a coffee and a bike
u1l1-3.explanation: With high inflation, money you keep buys less every year: it stops being a good store of value.

u1l1-4.prompt: Someone who earns €4,000 a month and spends it all can have a lower net worth than someone who earns €1,500 and saves €300.
u1l1-4.explanation: Net worth grows with what you save and invest, not with what you earn.

u1l1-5.prompt: Is it income or net worth?
options: The rent you collect every month
u1l1-5.explanation: Income is what comes in; net worth is what you build up.

u1l1-7.prompt: Net worth = what you own − what you ____.
u1l1-7.explanation: Debts subtract: a €15,000 car with a €12,000 loan only adds €3,000 to you.

u1l2-1.prompt: With 3 % inflation for 20 years, how much will €1,000 buy in today's euros? (round it)
u1l2-1.explanation: 1,000 ÷ 1.03²⁰ ≈ €554. Every year prices rise and the same money buys less.

u1l2-2.explanation: It's 2 % in the medium term. That's why idle money loses value even in normal years.

u1l2-3.prompt: By the rule of 70, 2 % inflation halves purchasing power in about ____ years.

u1l2-4.prompt: What can push prices up? Tick all that apply.
options: The central bank raising rates sharply
A lot of money being created very quickly
Far more demand than there are products
u1l2-4.explanation: Raising rates is precisely how inflation is curbed: it makes credit dearer and cools demand.

u1l2-5.prompt: Match each situation with its effect on prices.
options: Everyone wants to buy at once
u1l2-5.explanation: Cost-push inflation, demand-pull inflation and the ECB's tool for curbing both.

u1l2-6.prompt: It's 2022: inflation in Spain hits 8 % and your account pays 0 %. You have €10,000 you won't need for 10 years. What do you do?
options: Look into options that at least aim to beat inflation in the long run
Nothing: money in the bank is safe
Spend it all before it's worth less
u1l2-6.explanation: Idle money isn't safe from inflation. Money you won't need for years should be put to work.
feedback: Good: over 10 years, leaving it idle is the surest way to lose purchasing power.
Your €10,000 buys 8 % less in a year: about €800 of purchasing power gone.
Spending out of fear doesn't protect your future: it just swaps saving for consumption.

u1l2-7.prompt: Quick: 7 % inflation. In how many years does your money buy half as much (rule of 70)?

options: How much the prices of a consumer basket change
What a household earns on average
u1l3-1.explanation: It's a consumer price index: it compares the same basket over time.

u1l3-3.prompt: Your personal inflation can differ from the official figure.
u1l3-3.explanation: The CPI weights items by average spending; your basket gives each thing a different weight.

u1l3-5.prompt: If electricity shoots up one month, headline CPI jumps a lot, but ____ inflation barely moves.
u1l3-5.explanation: Core inflation excludes energy to show the underlying trend.

u1l3-6.prompt: A basket cost €200 a year ago and costs €206 today. What has the inflation of that basket been?

u1l3-7.prompt: Match each profile with the part of the basket that affects them most.
u1l3-7.explanation: Every household has its own basket: that's why personal inflation varies.

u1l3-9.prompt: What's true about the CPI? Tick all.
options: It compares prices with the same month the year before
Each product is weighted by average household spending
The INE publishes it every month
u1l3-9.explanation: The CPI is a weighted average of consumer prices.

u1l4-1.prompt: Your account pays 1.5 % and inflation is 2.7 %. What's your approximate real return?
u1l4-1.explanation: Real ≈ 1.5 − 2.7 = −1.2 %. You gain euros but lose purchasing power.

u1l4-2.prompt: If your account pays 3 % and inflation is 2 %, you gain purchasing power.

u1l4-3.prompt: Inflation at 2.5 %. Do you gain or lose purchasing power?
u1l4-3.explanation: You only gain if you earn more than inflation.

u1l4-4.prompt: What does the Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos (Spain's deposit guarantee scheme) protect?
options: Up to €100,000 per person per bank if the bank goes bust
u1l4-4.explanation: It protects the euros you've deposited if the bank goes bust, not against inflation or stock market falls.

u1l4-5.prompt: You have €20,000 in an account paying 0 % and won't need it for 15 years. A friend says: «That way you don't lose anything». What do you say?
options: That I should put it all in a single share
He's right: the balance doesn't go down
That I lose purchasing power every year
u1l4-5.explanation: Money sitting still for years = lost purchasing power.
feedback: That's going from one extreme to the other: later on you'll see why to diversify.
The balance doesn't go down, but with 2.5 % inflation that €20,000 will buy what about €13,800 buys today in 15 years.
Exactly: you don't lose euros, you lose what you can buy with them.

u1l4-6.explanation: It's the quick way to tell whether your money is gaining or losing purchasing power.

u1l5-1.prompt: €1,000 at 7 % compound interest for 30 years: what does it turn into? (round it)
u1l5-1.explanation: 1,000 × 1.07³⁰ ≈ €7,612. With simple interest it would be €3,100.

u1l5-3.prompt: Match each case with the type of interest.
options: You always earn on what you put in
You also earn on what you've already earned
A credit card debt that grows on itself
u1l5-3.explanation: Compounding speeds up growth… including the growth of debts.

u1l5-4.prompt: €10,000 at 5 % compound for 10 years: how much does it come to? (round to euros)
u1l5-4.explanation: 10,000 × 1.05¹⁰ ≈ €16,289. With simple interest it would be €15,000.

u1l5-5.prompt: Compound interest only works in your favour.
u1l5-5.explanation: It works against you too: a revolving credit card at 20 % doubles the debt in under 4 years.

u1l5-6.prompt: Put in order from lowest to highest the result of €100 a month for 30 years.
u1l5-6.explanation: €36,000, €49,273, €83,226 and €121,997: a few points of return make a huge difference to the end result.

u1l5-7.prompt: You're 22 and have €50 a month to invest. What do you do?
options: Spend it: €50 won't get you anywhere
Start now with €50 and raise the amount when I can
Wait until I earn more to start with something «serious»
u1l5-7.explanation: Starting early, even with a little, is what makes the most of compound interest.
feedback: €50 a month at 7 % for 40 years comes to about €130,000, with €24,000 put in.
Good: with time on your side, starting early matters more than starting big.
Waiting is costly: the early years are the ones with the most time to compound.

u1l6-1.prompt: By the rule of 72, at 6 % a year money doubles in about ____ years.

u1l6-2.prompt: At 9 % a year, how many years does it take money to double according to the rule of 72?

u1l6-4.prompt: Match each return with the years it takes to double.

u1l6-6.prompt: A revolving credit card charges 24 % a year. In how many years does the debt double if you don't pay?
u1l6-6.explanation: 72 ÷ 24 = 3 years. Compound interest also works for your creditor.

u1l6-7.prompt: The rule of 72 also works for inflation: at 3 %, prices double in about 24 years.

u1l6-8.prompt: To double your money in under 10 years, what return do you need?
u1l6-8.explanation: Under 10 years requires more than 7.2 % a year (72 ÷ 10).
